reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes joining a purported millionaire team and presents OneCoin as a money-making business opportunity involving token packages, later sales, mining-pool participation, projected appreciation, and team-based rewards. It also connects access to a payment platform with requests for bank identification, account information, and an electricity bill, although no document submission, transaction, or return is established.

then enter the mining pool with your tokens

opening.argument: Judge the forecast as a forecast, not a promised return. The presentation asks whether OneCoin is legal and whether promoting it could cause problems, putting those questions before the audience rather than treating them as irrelevant. Its projected value is expressly conditional on participants' commitment, and the growth chart labels its figures as predictions. That does not establish the forecast is sound, but it weakens the claim that viewers are given an unconditional assurance of profit.

these values can then be achieved if the commitment from all of us is on the right side

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited references to paying for packs and using tokens for mining describe participation, but neither quote promises a fixed payout. The identification passage describes a stated platform requirement; it does not show anyone submitting documents. Even the matching-bonus slide describes a conditional qualification, not earnings already received. Those distinctions matter when deciding what this presentation actually establishes.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A conditional forecast is still being used to promote participation. The speaker links obtaining packages to tokens, urges viewers to secure mining places, and says that mining generates profit. The absence of a fixed payout does not erase the paid pathway into purported returns, while asking about legality does not answer that question.

opening.argument: Much of the webinar walks through concepts and operations: the presenter invites questions, describes study documents, videos and quizzes, and recommends completing training and examinations before trading. The exchange slide shows the interface being discussed. Read in that context, explanations of tokens and mining can be understood as part of a course and platform demonstration, rather than proof that the audience is being asked to pay immediately.

citations.quote: At the end of the webinar we will then ask you some questions and then you all can ask your questions.
It's about getting the knowledge from the, from study documents to videos, and thus of course get more and more knowledge.
I recommend to everyone really do the training first take the examinations off and then only start playing around with the topic which buy or sell on the exchange

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening cites pack payments and mining mechanics, but an operational lesson would naturally explain both. Its bank-document quote likewise describes an account procedure, without establishing that a viewer handed over documents. The matching-bonus slide is evidence of a feature presented in the webinar, not evidence that anyone received a bonus. The instructional sequence and advice to train before trading deserve weight.

I recommend to everyone really do the training first take the examinations off

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The lessons are embedded in a solicitation. The description asks viewers to join and sign up; the presenter says to obtain a training package quickly to participate in the promotion. The closing slide calls for buying and selling tokens and entering the mining pool. Teaching viewers how to use the system does not make those invitations merely educational.

citations.quote: Join the millionaire team!!!!!! Signup free now:
If you can participate in the promotion, you should take care of the training package as quickly as possible

opening.argument: The described offering also includes training levels, tests, an exchange interface and an account-verification process. Those can be read as services with participation requirements. The speaker even says some tokens can be earned through tests, while the identification request is framed as a platform requirement. The cited material does not establish that a viewer deposited money, submitted documents, received a return or suffered a loss. A judge should distinguish the offer's claims from proof of an actual transaction or outcome.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening correctly identifies references to paid packs, mining and team rewards, but the quoted passages do not establish a completed purchase, a delivered coin or a paid bonus. The bank-identification passage does not establish document submission either. Those limits do not validate the service; they limit what can be concluded from this recording alone.

citations.quote: usually you would pay for your packs
you need six tokens to return a ready-made one-coin
One Pay Platform required a bank ID, bank have a regular bank account. And a electricity bill.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A completed transaction is not necessary to identify what the video promotes. Its speaker connects packages to token acquisition and mining, explicitly attributes profit to mining, and the matching-bonus slide offers earnings tied to a team and package qualification. Free tokens for successful tests do not negate that paid route or the recruitment incentive.
